name: Omar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My brother Yusuf and I farm Santos Brothers, two hundred hectares, half ours and half rented. We finish beef cattle, about a hundred and fifty a year, and grow wheat and barley, mostly to feed them. I do the cattle and the books, Yusuf does the machinery and the crops. And this year we've got my nephew Mateo with us as an apprentice, he's nineteen and keen as mustard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does an ordinary day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, feed round in the sheds, check the water and the troughs. Mid-morning I'm in the office with a coffee doing the cattle passports and the orders, and I'll sometimes ask the AI on the laptop to explain a new rule in plain words, because the official letters never do. Afternoons I'm with Mateo, showing him how to handle cattle without getting hurt. My wife Amira runs the farm accounts on Fridays and keeps us honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. I've always said it was a useful tool, not a miracle. Like the GPS on the tractor, good, but you still need a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who promised the moon should be a bit quieter now. A tool is a tool, and the farmers who use them sensibly will do well. That's what I'd say at the mart or the church breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan holds. Teach Mateo, hand more of the cattle over to him, and ease off at sixty-five or so. Yusuf's three years younger, he'll carry on a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep using the AI now and then for the forms. I'd buy a second-hand cattle crush, the gate that holds an animal still for the vet, because ours is twenty-five years old. And I'd keep Mateo on and get him through his apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the world I know, and I know how to farm in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why second-hand? Is that a money thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. A new one is nine thousand, a good used one is four. But mostly, if a crush has lasted five years on someone else's farm, I know it works. I don't like being the first to buy anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you most want Mateo to learn from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To read cattle. When a bullock's about to kick, when one's off its food, when one's just being awkward. You learn it by being stood next to someone who knows, there's no other way.

S0.say: I'd say the people who promised the moon should be a bit quieter now. A tool is a tool, and the farmers who use them sensibly will do well.
S0.think: My plan holds: teach my nephew, hand more of the cattle to him and ease off around sixty-five. My brother, three years younger, will carry on a bit longer.
S0.do: Carries on and keeps using AI now and then for official forms. Buys a second-hand cattle crush for about four thousand and keeps his nephew on through his apprenticeship.
S0.feel: Calm, in a world he knows how to farm in.
S0.quote: A new one is nine thousand, a good used one is four. But mostly, if a crush has lasted five years on someone else's farm, I know it works.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is measured and practical, and his way of handling change is to let others prove it first. Teaching his nephew is clearly the centre of his working life now. He uses AI only to translate official letters into plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, if I'm honest. Things change, but not overnight, which is how farming has always gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it always is, new machines come and the good farmers adapt. My grandfather went from horses to tractors and nobody needed a government programme for it. Learn the new ways, work hard, and don't wait for someone to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I wonder what it means for Mateo. If machines do the feeding and the field work, what's left to apprentice in? I'd want him learning the new kit alongside the old skills, or I'm teaching him a trade that won't be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two and see what the bigger beef farms buy and how it works out. Then I'd buy what's proven, probably a feed-pushing robot or cameras in the sheds, second-hand if possible. I'd send Mateo on whatever course the college runs on the new kit, and I'd use the AI more for the office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not for me, for the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your grandfather going from horses to tractors. What did that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He kept one horse for years after, a big grey called Captain, for carting in the wet. My father said he never trusted a tractor in a muddy gateway. I'm probably the same with robots, I'll keep something old around just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the change pushed beef prices down, who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the machines. The supermarkets, maybe, and the rules that make it hard for small farms to sell direct. Let us sell to whoever we like, and we'll be fine.

S1.say: I'd say new machines always come and good farmers adapt, as my grandfather did from horses to tractors without a government programme. Learn the new ways, work hard and don't wait to be rescued.
S1.think: I wonder what it means for my apprentice nephew, if machines do the feeding and fieldwork. I'd want him learning the new kit alongside the old skills, or I'm teaching a trade that won't be there.
S1.do: Waits a year or two to see what bigger beef farms buy, then buys proven kit such as a feed-pushing robot or shed cameras, second-hand if possible. Sends his nephew on a college course on the new kit and uses AI more for office work.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy, not for himself but for his nephew.
S1.quote: I'm probably the same with robots, I'll keep something old around just in case.
S1.fieldNote: Omar's public line is self-reliance and he frames change through his family's history. Underneath, his concern is entirely about his apprentice. He blames supermarkets and rules, not technology, which fits his free-market view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. No. That's too fast for anyone to adapt, I don't care how hard they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say people need to stand on their own feet, but I'd admit this is different. Nobody can work their way out of something that hits in two years. I'd say families and churches need to pull together, because that's who'll actually be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the beef price would fall through the floor, because robot farms could finish cattle for half our cost. We own half our land, so we wouldn't lose everything, but the rented half would go to whoever pays more. And Mateo's apprenticeship would be finished before it's started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Yusuf and I would sit down with Amira and the accounts and cut everything we could. I'd hand back the rented land at the next renewal and run fewer cattle on our own half. I'd talk to my sister about Mateo, and maybe help him look at a different trade, something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying awake running the numbers again and again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo, face to face?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's done nothing wrong and he's a good stockman, and that's true. Then I'd tell him the honest bit, that I can't promise there's a job here in two years. That would be one of the hardest things I've said to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said don't wait for rescue, but in this one would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it helped the farm survive, I'd take it, and I'd not enjoy saying so. What I'd want is help to keep working, not money for nothing. A grant to diversify, maybe, not a cheque in the post.

S2.say: I'd still say people must stand on their own feet, but admit nobody can work their way out of something that hits in two years. Families and churches would need to pull together, because they're who'll actually be there.
S2.think: The beef price would collapse because robot farms could finish cattle at half our cost. We own half our land so we wouldn't lose everything, but the rented half would go and my nephew's apprenticeship would end before it started.
S2.do: Sits down with his brother and wife to cut every cost possible. Hands back the rented land at the next renewal, runs fewer cattle and helps his nephew look at a different trade that works with people.
S2.feel: Anxious, lying awake running the numbers.
S2.quote: Then I'd tell him the honest bit, that I can't promise there's a job here in two years.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario forces Omar to admit that self-reliance has limits, and he says so openly. He would shrink the farm to the land they own rather than fight. Telling his nephew the truth is the moment he dreads most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight but workable. Five years is two apprenticeships, near enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for families and farms to get ready, not for crying about it. Teach the young ones the new skills, keep what works, and buy smart. I'd say it at the mart and to the young farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd get through it. We'd have time to see which robots work on beef farms, buy them once they're proven, and make Mateo the one who runs them. Yusuf and I would be in our sixties and could step back gradually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign Mateo up for the college's robotics and data course on top of his apprenticeship, and pay half. By year two or three I'd buy whatever kit the neighbours have proven, probably second-hand. I'd keep the rented land for now, but get the lease terms shorter so we can hand it back if we need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. I sleep better with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paying half the course isn't cheap. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the money I'd have spent on the new crush, ha. The old one can last three more years if Yusuf welds it again. Mateo's worth more than a gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with five years compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. With two I'm cutting and shrinking. With five I'm building, just carefully, the way we've always done it.

S3.say: I'd say it's time for families and farms to get ready, not cry about it: teach the young ones new skills, keep what works and buy smart. I'd say it at the mart and to the young farmers.
S3.think: We'd get through it, with time to see which robots work on beef farms, buy them once proven and make my nephew the one who runs them. My brother and I could step back gradually in our sixties.
S3.do: Signs his nephew up for the college robotics and data course and pays half, using money meant for the cattle crush. Buys proven kit, probably second-hand, by year two or three and shortens the lease terms on rented land.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a plan, which helps him sleep.
S3.quote: The old one can last three more years if Yusuf welds it again. Mateo's worth more than a gate.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Omar switches from shrinking to building, slowly and on proven ground. He puts money into his nephew's training before kit, which says a lot about his priorities. His caution is a method, not a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway. I'd be sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready. Ten years is long enough to learn a trade, pay off debts and set up the next generation. If people are caught out in ten years, that's on them, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits us. I'd hand the cattle to Mateo by sixty-five and step back, and he'd be the one making the robot decisions with Yusuf. I'd still worry a little about the beef price, but I'd have done my part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now for a few years and keep teaching Mateo the old ways and the new. I'd buy kit gradually, once it's been proven on other farms. I'd save steadily and plan to hand over to Mateo at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Pleased, even, that there's time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if people are caught out, that's on them, mostly. Who's the mostly for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones without family, I suppose. A sixty-year-old who's worked one farm all his life with no son to hand over to, that's hard. I'd not say it's on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the handover day look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A meal at our house with Amira's cooking, Yusuf and his wife, Mateo and his mother. I'd give him the keys to the cattle shed and my old stick. He'd probably laugh at the stick, but he'd keep it.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready, because ten years is long enough to learn a trade, pay off debts and set up the next generation. If people are caught out, that's mostly on them.
S4.think: It suits us: I'd hand the cattle to my nephew by sixty-five and he'd make the robot decisions with my brother. I'd still worry a little about the beef price, but I'd have done my part.
S4.do: Carries on for a few years while teaching his nephew both old and new methods. Buys kit gradually once proven on other farms, saves steadily and plans to hand over at sixty-five.
S4.feel: Mostly calm and pleased there's time to do it properly.
S4.quote: I'd give him the keys to the cattle shed and my old stick. He'd probably laugh at the stick, but he'd keep it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Omar is calm and his family succession plan works. When pressed on his tough line about people being caught out, he softened it for older workers without family. The handover meal he described is warm and specific.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to bring Mateo through. What would help is grants to retrain young people and diversify, things you earn by working, and fewer rules stopping small farms selling their own beef direct.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the brothers. Yusuf and I have farmed side by side for thirty years and never had a contract between us. When things get hard, it's family that holds, not paper.

headlineQuote: When things get hard, it's family that holds, not paper.
portrait: Omar Santos is a 58-year-old beef and cereal farmer who runs two hundred hectares, half owned and half rented, with his younger brother Yusuf, while his wife Amira keeps the accounts. He uses AI now and then to decode official letters, buys kit second-hand once others have proven it, and is training his nineteen-year-old nephew Mateo as an apprentice. He believes in self-reliance and family over government, but admits the two-year scenario is too fast for anyone to work through and would take help to save the farm. With five or ten years he builds carefully, pays for Mateo's training in the new kit and plans to hand over the cattle at sixty-five.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because there would be no time to bring his apprentice nephew through.
whatWouldHelp: Grants to retrain young people and diversify that are earned by working, and fewer rules stopping small farms from selling their own beef direct.
